messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy-one-year-old Henry still remembers the smell of his father's whiskey-soaked breath as he towered over him, fists clenched. The abuse had been a regular occurrence throughout Henry's childhood, leaving an indelible mark on his psyche. Even now, the scent of alcohol wafting from a passerby or a TV show can transport him back to those terrifying moments. As Henry navigates his daily routine as an insurance agent, he finds himself increasingly anxious when interacting with strangers. He becomes acutely aware of their proximity, tone, and body language, often misinterpreting innocuous gestures as potential threats. This hypervigilance stems from the deep-seated conviction that those responsible for his childhood trauma have faced no consequences, leaving him feeling perpetually vulnerable. The lack of accountability weighs heavily on Henry's mind, fueling his perception that strangers pose an imminent danger. To cope with these feelings, Henry has developed a repertoire of mental rituals aimed at preventing similar traumas from recurring. He keeps his mind occupied by mentally rearranging insurance policies or replaying past conversations ad infinitum. This distraction serves as a fragile shield against the memories that threaten to resurface at any moment. When fragments of those traumatic events do suddenly reappear, Henry is overwhelmed by their vividness and the accompanying sensory details – like the smell of his father's whiskey. As he tries to make sense of these intrusive recollections, Henry becomes increasingly convinced that his body is betraying him by reacting as if danger lurks around every corner. He finds himself "on edge" even in mundane situations, listening intently for sounds that might signal an intruder. The sirens blaring outside his office window can send his heart racing, and the mere thought of someone approaching him triggers a cascade of worst-case scenarios. Henry's attempts to avoid media coverage of similar events only serve to reinforce his conviction that he is not safe. He becomes trapped in a cycle of avoidance and hypervigilance, with each perceived threat fuelling his determination to prevent future traumas through mental rituals and distraction. This self-reinforcing loop has taken a toll on Henry's relationships and daily life, ultimately driving him to seek help. Despite the overwhelming sense of vulnerability that haunts him, Henry is most afraid of losing control – of succumbing to the memories that continue to assail him. He hopes that therapy will provide a safe space for him to confront these demons and break free from the maladaptive strategies that have come to define his existence. As he takes this first tentative step towards healing, Henry can't help but wonder if it's already too late – or if he'll finally be able to find some measure of peace after decades of living in fear.
